utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Let the Registrar call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning Your Honour. Case number IT-95-8-I, the Prosecutor versus Damir Dosen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. The appearances.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Please Your Honour, my name is Niemann. I appear with my colleague, Mr. Kapila Waidyaratne, and the case manager, Patrica Reynders.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: My name is Vladimir Petrovic. I am an attorney from Belgrade and I represent Mr. Dosen in this case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: This is the adjourned initial appearance of this accused, adjourned from last week. The amended indictment was confirmed in this case on the 30th of August of this year. Mr. Petrovic, I take it that your client has received a copy of the amended indictment in a language which he understands and that you've had the opportunity of going through it with him? Counsel who was here last week undertook to do that; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: That is right, Your Honour. My client received a copy of the indictment in Serbian language. We had an opportunity to read through it entirely. Mr. Dosen has understood the indictment. He understands what he is charged with and he is prepared to make a plea today on all the charges in the indictment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. The final matter is this, before we deal with the indictment: Does he wish to have the indictment read out in full or is he prepared to waive that right? As you know, there is a right to have the indictment read out in full, but frequently it's waived to save time.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: I spoke to Mr. Dosen regarding this matter. It is sufficient that only the counts be read out without reading the indictment in its entirety. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. Let the accused stand. Mr. Dosen, you've heard what your counsel has said, that you've had the indictment in a language you understand. You've been through it with him, and you are in a position to enter pleas today; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Now, I am going to read to you the counts in the indictment, and to each you must enter a plea. Kindly confine your answers to "guilty" or "not guilty." The first three counts relate to alleged offences between the 24th of May and the 30th of August 1992 in Keraterm Camp. Count 1: Persecutions on political, racial or religious grounds, crime against humanity, punishable under Articles 5(h), 7(1) and 7(3) of the Statute of the Tribunal. How do you plead, guilty or not guilty?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: No, not guilty.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Count 2: Inhumane acts, a crime against humanity, punishable under Articles 5(i), 7(1), 7(3) of the Statute. How do you plead, guilty or not guilty?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Not guilty.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Count 3: Outrages upon personal dignity, violations of the laws or customs of war as recognised by Article (3)(a)(c) of the Geneva Conventions of 1949, punishable under Articles 3, 7(1) and 7(3) of the Statute of the Tribunal. How do you plead, guilty or not guilty?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Not guilty.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Counts 4 to 7 relate to alleged offences on or about the 25th of June 1992 in room 2 of the camp. Count 4: Torture, a crime against humanity, punishable under Articles 5(f), 7(1) and 7(3) of the Statute. How do you plead, guilty or not guilty?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Not guilty.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Count 5: Torture, a violation of the laws or customs of war recognised by Article (3)(1)(a) of the Geneva Conventions of 1949, punishable under Articles 3, 7(1) and 7(3) of the Statute. How do you plead, guilty or not guilty?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Not guilty.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Count 6: Inhumane acts, a crime against humanity punishable under Articles 5(i), 7(1) and 7(3) of the Statute. How do you plead, guilty or not guilty?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Not guilty.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Count 7: Cruel treatment, a violation of the laws or customs of war recognised by Article (3)(1)(a) of the Geneva Conventions of 1949 punishable under Articles 3, 7(1) and 7(3) of the Statute. How do you plead, guilty or not guilty?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Not guilty.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. You may be seated.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Niemann, that concludes the putting the indictment.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: This matter, clearly, is in no position at the moment to proceed, but it may be sensible to do what we can, if anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The accused -- the defence have had all the material, have they?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: The confirmation material has been disclosed, Your Honour, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: There is another accused, of course, on this indictment.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: How do you propose to go on from here?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, it would be our submission that the matters should proceed together and that on all next occasions when the other accused is to come before the Tribunal, so should this accused, and the matter to proceed that way. I don't know at this stage what the position is with respect to when a hearing of the matter involving the accused Kolundzija will proceed, but I would imagine it would be sometime after the Kvocka case, Your Honour, so I think it may be some time. But we are in a position to make available the material in a reasonably timely manner and -- because both the cases are prepared for trial. So we can proceed rather quickly in that regard.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: What is the extent of this case? There are seven counts. How many witnesses are we looking at?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour. I can say it this way, Your Honour. Probably about 50 to 60 witnesses. The position is that the evidence is identical to the evidence that will be led against the accused Zigic in the other case and the accused Kolundzija and this accused, Your Honour. So it is the same evidence exactly in relation to the three accused. And we think about 50, 60 witnesses, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: So, what is that, four months for the Prosecution? Something of that order?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: A month, I think -- yes, I would imagine six weeks probably to dispose the Prosecution case, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, there will be a hearing in the case of the co-accused, I anticipate, certainly in January. I shall make some inquiries about that. Yes, there is no date at the moment for a Status Conference for the co-accused, but I anticipate there will be one towards the end of January, and it would be sensible for this accused to appear at the same time.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes, we would suggest that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It may require further amendments to the indictment? You have to produce a joint indictment.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I think the indictment has in fact been joined. There is a process, complicated as it is, but they were served individually, but there in fact exists one joint indictment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, but there are other people involved.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: They can't proceed to trial, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: So at some stage we shall need a new indictment on just these two?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Well, thank you very much. Is there anything else we can usefully do today?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I don't think so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic, you've heard what's suggested. This matter will have to proceed with the co-accused. There is a Status Conference in his case which will have to be fixed in January, and it would seem sensible for this accused to appear at the same time.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, indeed it does seem sensible. The only thing I would like to inquire is whether there will be a formal request on the part of the Prosecution to join the indictments, that is the indictments of Kolundzija and Dosen. That is one thing. Secondly, I have received some statements that it was about seven or eight witness statements. I would like to know whether this is the entire supporting material, whether I can consider that all the supporting material has been produced and whether from now on the clock is running as far as the preliminary motions are concerned on the part of the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, from what the Prosecution have said, the answer to that question is yes. Clearly, some sort of joint indictment also will have to be produced so that the two can be tried together. Your client did not appear last week because he was suffering from an injury sustained playing volleyball, as I understand it. He is now recovered, is he?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. That is correct. And today he -- since he still has pains in his back and he -- it was with some effort that he arrived in the Court today, because he is still in pain when they put on his flak jacket.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Is there anything else you want to raise, Mr. Petrovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: No, not really, except that if the Prosecution would specify whether this was the entire supporting material so far and whether the time for the preliminary motions is running as of today.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: That's right, Your Honour. That is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes is the answer, as I thought. Mr. Dosen, would you stand up, please. That concludes the initial appearance. As you've heard, there are various preliminary matters which have to be covered, various steps which have to be taken before your case will be ready for trial, and you will appear with your co-accused at a date which is to be fixed in January, which will be your next Court appearance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. We'll adjourn until then.
